claim: Every new attribute line is wrapped in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`, so nothing generated for netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework targets is decorated. `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` exists in netstandard2.0 and in .NET Framework 4.0+, and it can be applied to classes on both. The derived criterion only allows conditional emission where the attribute does not exist, and the requirement says ALL generated code is decorated. A common case is a library that targets only netstandard2.0 and is tested from a net8.0 test project: coverage is measured on the netstandard2.0 build, which still has none of the attributes. That is exactly the skew the requirement wants removed. The same guard appears in every template (Formatter, StringKeyFormatter, Enum, Union, Resolver, CompositeResolver and their .cs counterparts).

claim: Adding `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` unconditionally to the generated half of the user's own `partial` resolver class breaks existing code. Inputs: `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver]` or `[CompositeResolver(...)]` on a `partial class` that the user already marked `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]`, which is the obvious thing to do for a resolver class. `ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` is `AllowMultiple = false`, so on net5+/netcoreapp targets the merged declaration carries the attribute twice and fails with CS0579. Code that compiled on base no longer compiles. The generator does not check whether the user's declaration already has the attribute.

claim: The guard `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` drops the attribute on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework, which are the most common library targets. `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` exists in netstandard2.0 and in .NET Framework 4.0+, so the condition is too broad.
